questions.text: Two forces, of magnitudes 50 N and 80 N, act at a point on a Cartesian plane (50 N at 30 degrees above the horizontal, 80 N along the horizontal). 2.1 name the single vector with the same effect; 2.2 calculate the vertical component of the 50 N force, the magnitude of the resultant force, and its direction.

A 45 kg box is pulled with a 90 N force at 50 degrees to the horizontal and moves at CONSTANT VELOCITY. Define kinetic frictional force; state Newton's First Law; calculate the horizontal component of the applied force, the normal force, and the coefficient of kinetic friction.
State Newton's Second Law of Motion in words.
questions.memo_answer: When a resultant/net force acts on an object, the object will accelerate in the direction of the force. The acceleration is directly proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to the mass of the object.
questions.memo_note: Memo instruction: penalise -1 if key words/phrase omitted - exact CAPS wording matters.

questions.text: Learners plot the inverse of acceleration (1/a) against mass m for a constant net force. Calculate the gradient of the graph.
questions.memo_working: Accept any set of coordinates from the graph, e.g. (2,5 - 0)/(1,25 - 0) = 2 or (2,1 - 1,7)/(1,05 - 0,85) = 2

questions.text: Hence, determine the net force applied on the object during the experiment (graph of 1/a versus m, gradient 2).
questions.memo_working: From F_net = ma: 1/a = m/F_net, so gradient = 1/F_net = 2, giving F_net = 1/2 = 0,5 N. (Memo option 2: F_net = ma = (1)(1/2) = 0,5 N.)

questions.text: Write down a conclusion for this experiment.
questions.memo_answer: Acceleration is inversely proportional to the mass of an object (if the net force is kept constant).

questions.text: A 25 kg crate slides down a plane inclined at 15 degrees: frictionless from A to B, rough from B to C. Draw a free-body diagram; calculate the acceleration A to B; give the direction of acceleration B to C; given net acceleration 1,2 m/s^2 from B to C, calculate the frictional force.

The gravitational force on the Curiosity probe on Mars is 3 338 N; radius of Mars 3 390 km, mass 6,39 x 10^23 kg. State Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation; calculate the probe's mass and its weight on Earth.
